STEP 0: LEARN THE REPOSITORY BEFORE WRITING
1. If `dump.txt` exists (project files or repo root), read it first. Then read `README.md` and `content/authors/`.
2. Read the source of `BookCompiler`, `QuestionCompiler`, and `SyntaxHighlighter`. Extract the exact rules for: file and folder naming, required and optional YAML keys, question schema, allowed `type` values, how `correct` is parsed, whether block scalars (`|-`) are accepted, and the exact list of supported code-fence languages.
3. Read two existing books under `content/books/` (if any) and copy their style, `author` id, and `date` format. Use the author id `terlingua-team` if it exists in `content/authors/`; otherwise use the author id most common in existing `book.yml` files.
4. Source-of-truth order when rules conflict: compiler source > existing books > this prompt. Log every conflict in NOTES.md.
5. RESUME LOGIC: if `_build/networking-and-protocols/progress.md` or any files under `content/books/networking-and-protocols/` already exist, read them, keep valid work, and continue from the first unfinished section instead of starting over.

WORKFLOW (follow in order)
1. PLAN: write `_build/networking-and-protocols/plan.md` with the full table of contents (chapter folder names, section file names, one-line learning goal per section, and the 5–7 question concepts per section so no concept repeats across sections). 3–5 sections per chapter; Chapter 7 may have 3–4 review sections. 3. WRITE: create `book.yml`, each `chapter.yml`, then every section file, one at a time, saving each to disk immediately. Do not skip, stub, abbreviate, or leave placeholders. Never write "and so on" or "similar for the rest".
4. VALIDATE: write `_build/networking-and-protocols/validate.py` (Python, using PyYAML or ruamel if installable, otherwise a careful parser) and run it. It must check every rule in "HARD FORMAT RULES" below and the answer-position distribution. Repeat until clean.

MATH AUDIT: write `_build/networking-and-protocols/check_math.py` using Python's `ipaddress` module and plain arithmetic to recompute every CIDR boundary, host count, longest-prefix match, MTU/MSS value, sequence/ACK number, RTT total, bandwidth-delay product, and window or throughput figure used in the book. 7. QUESTION AUDIT: re-read every question. Confirm that exactly the options marked `correct: true` are correct, that every distractor is actually wrong, that the explanation agrees with the marks, and that the answer is derivable from the section's prose plus the explanation. Fix problems in place.

HARD FORMAT RULES (verify against the compiler; the compiler wins)
Files:
- `content/books/<slug>/book.yml`: `title`, `author`, `summary`, `date`, `tags`, `draft: false`.
- Chapter folders `NN-chapter-slug/` containing `chapter.yml` (`title`, `summary`, `draft: false`).
- Section files `NN-subchapter-slug.md` inside chapter folders. Names use lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens only.
Front matter of every section: `title` and `questions` (5–7 questions).
Each question has: `id`, `prompt`, `type`, `explanation`, `options`.
- `id`: unique lowercase slug within the section (letters, digits, hyphens). NEVER `yes`, `no`, `true`, `false`, `null` (any case).
- `type`: ALWAYS present, either `single` (exactly 1 correct option) or `multiple` (2–3 correct options out of 5; the prompt must end with "Select all that apply.").
- `options`: 4–5 items; each has `text`; right answers also have `correct: true`; wrong answers have no `correct` key.
- `explanation`: required on every question and fully self-contained. Structure: (a) why the correct option(s) hold, citing the RFC and rule; (b) why EACH distractor fails, naming the specific misconception; (c) all subnetting, MTU, RTT, window, or bandwidth-delay arithmetic step by step. Refer to options by their text, NEVER by letter or position (e.g., never "option B").
YAML safety:
- Double-quote every string value (`title`, `id`, `prompt`, option `text`, `summary`, etc.). Escape inner double quotes. This avoids boolean/number/null coercion and `: ` / ` #` / leading `` ` `` `@` `[` `{` `*` `- ` problems (e.g., option text `"200"`, `"404"`, `"No"`).
- Long explanations: use a block scalar (`explanation: |-` with indented lines) if the compiler or existing books accept it; otherwise a double-quoted string. Test with the real compiler on the first section before writing the rest.
- Never put `---` at the start of a line inside front matter content.
Markdown body:
- The body starts with `## Learning objectives` (3–5 bullets), then the structure below.
- Every fenced code block has a language tag from this set, intersected with what `SyntaxHighlighter` supports: `csharp`, `python`, `javascript`, `sql`, `bash`, `json`, `yaml`, `html`. Show raw HTTP messages, DNS zone snippets, and packet captures as `bash` blocks (or Markdown tables for header and field layouts) unless the highlighter supports a better tag. Keep snippets short and exact.
Answer-position balance (the UI does not shuffle): for question number k (1-based) in section number s of the book, place the first correct option at index ((k + s) mod n), 0-based, where n is that question's option count; for `multiple` questions, place correct options at that index and the next valid index(es). validate.py must verify that no position holds more than 40% of the correct answers within any section.

SECTION STRUCTURE (400–1200 words of prose per section, one crisp concept each)
1. `## Learning objectives`
2. `## The invariant` : the timeless mechanism, stated precisely, with the RFC rule behind it.
3. `## Worked example` : concrete numbers, a packet or message trace, or a short code sample with exact expected output.
4. `## Where this shows up today` : the relevance block (see policy below).
5. `## Pitfalls checklist` : 3–6 bullets of mistakes engineers actually make.
6. `## Key takeaways` : 3–5 bullets.

TIMELESS-VS-CURRENT POLICY (apply strictly)
- At most ONE question per section may depend on a fact that could change within five years (adoption levels, defaults, deployment status). All other questions must rest on invariants: protocol state machines, header semantics, arithmetic, RFC-defined behavior.
- The "Where this shows up today" block is at most about 15% of the section. It connects the invariant to how the world looks in 2026: current deployments, defaults, and trends. Every dated claim must be written as "As of November 2026, ..." and, if it names a product, library, or version, include it. Name products only as examples of a mechanism, never as the point.
- If web access is available, verify every dated claim against primary sources (RFC Editor, IETF datatracker, vendor and browser release notes, CA/Browser Forum documents, registry or measurement sites you can read) before writing it. If you cannot verify a current-state claim, drop it or restate it as a general mechanism. Never guess adoption percentages, versions, or dates.
- Citations: cite RFC numbers throughout; add a section number only when you have confirmed it in the RFC text. Never fabricate a quote or section number. Distinguish what the RFC mandates (MUST), recommends (SHOULD), and what implementations commonly do.
- Dated facts must never be the only reason an answer is correct.

QUESTION QUALITY RULES
- Mix per section: at least 2 compute-or-trace questions, at least 1 "spot the bug / what happens next" question, and the rest conceptual or scenario-based.
- Distractors are real misconceptions, plausible and parallel in length and style; the correct option must not be systematically the longest.
- No "all of the above" or "none of the above". No trick wording. No negations in stems unless emphasized with NOT.
- Every question must be answerable using only what that section teaches plus the explanation. No concept is tested twice across the whole book except in Chapter 7 (review), which must combine concepts from earlier chapters.
- Prompts are Markdown; use inline code for identifiers and values.

EXEMPLAR (shape only; do not copy its content)
````markdown
---
title: "Integer Division Truncation"
questions:
  - id: "negative-division"
    type: "single"
    prompt: "In C#, what does `-7 / 2` evaluate to?"
    explanation: |-
      C# integer division truncates toward zero, so the exact quotient -3.5 becomes -3.
      "-4" is what floor division would give (as in Python's `//`), but C# does not floor.
      "-3.5" is wrong because both operands are `int`, so the result is `int`.
      "4" ignores the sign entirely.
      Arithmetic: 7 / 2 = 3 remainder 1, so |quotient| = 3; the sign is negative, giving -3.
    options:
      - text: "-4"
      - text: "-3"
        correct: true
      - text: "-3.5"
      - text: "4"
---

## Learning objectives

- Predict the result of integer division for negative operands.

## The invariant
````

BOOK SPECIFICATION
- Slug: networking-and-protocols
- Title: "Networking & Internet Protocols: RFC Mechanics"
- Summary: "The protocol invariants behind IP routing, TCP congestion control, QUIC, DNS, TLS 1.3, and HTTP semantics — verifiable against the RFCs, with concrete latency and throughput math."
- Tags: [networking, protocols, tcp, http, dns, tls]
- Author/date: author id per Step 0; `date` = 2026-11-27 in the repo's date format.
- Audience: working software engineers who build networked services but have not read the RFCs. Prerequisites: binary and hexadecimal, basic programming, having used HTTP APIs.
- Primary sources to cite where relevant: RFC 791 and RFC 8200 (IP), RFC 4632 (CIDR), RFC 826 and RFC 4861 (ARP/NDP), RFC 1191 and RFC 8201 (PMTUD), RFC 9293 (TCP), RFC 5681 (congestion control), RFC 6298 (RTO), RFC 9000/9001/9002 (QUIC), RFC 9114 (HTTP/3), RFC 9110/9111/9112/9113 (HTTP), RFC 1034/1035/2181/2308 (DNS), RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3), RFC 5280 (X.509), RFC 6455 (WebSocket). Confirm each is current before citing.

Chapters (folder names fixed; choose 3–5 sections for each):
01-layering-addressing-and-routing: OSI as a teaching model vs the TCP/IP hourglass; link-layer vs network-layer addressing and how MAC addresses change per hop while IP addresses stay end to end; ARP and NDP; IPv4 and IPv6 essentials; CIDR arithmetic, subnet boundaries, summarization, longest-prefix match; NAT and port exhaustion; MTU, MSS, fragmentation, Path MTU Discovery and ICMP black holes. Today: IPv6 deployment and carrier-grade NAT as the practical consequence of IPv4 exhaustion (verify current adoption from a primary measurement source or omit numbers).
02-tcp-state-flow-and-congestion: three-way handshake, sequence and ACK arithmetic, teardown and TIME_WAIT (2*MSL), flow control (rwnd) vs congestion control (cwnd), slow start, AIMD, fast retransmit and recovery, RTO estimation, bandwidth-delay product, Nagle plus delayed-ACK interaction, transport-layer head-of-line blocking. Today: loss-based vs model-based congestion control (e.g., CUBIC and BBR) as a mechanism-level contrast; verify defaults before naming them.
03-udp-quic-and-http3: UDP as message-framed and connectionless; QUIC's stream multiplexing, per-stream loss recovery, connection IDs and migration, 1-RTT and 0-RTT handshakes and replay risk, QUIC's integration with TLS 1.3, why QUIC runs over UDP (middlebox ossification). Today: HTTP/3 and QUIC deployment on major browsers and CDNs; UDP blocking in enterprise networks and fallback to TCP (verify claims).
04-dns-resolution-and-caching-invariants: root, TLD, authoritative hierarchy; recursive vs iterative resolution; record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SRV, NS, PTR, SOA); why a CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name (zone apex consequences, ALIAS/ANAME as provider-specific workarounds); positive TTL vs negative caching (SOA minimum, RFC 2308); anycast; DNSSEC basics at the concept level. Today: encrypted DNS transports (DoH, DoT), the SVCB/HTTPS record types and what they enable (verify RFC numbers and status).
05-tls-13-and-trust-chains: confidentiality vs integrity vs authenticity; the TLS 1.3 handshake in 1-RTT; ECDHE and forward secrecy; AEAD record protection; X.509 chain validation steps, trust anchors, revocation concepts; SNI and ALPN; what TLS does not hide (IP addresses, SNI unless Encrypted Client Hello, sizes and timing); 0-RTT replay. Today: certificate lifetime reductions and automated issuance (ACME), ECH status, and hybrid post-quantum key exchange in TLS (verify each from IETF and CA/Browser Forum or vendor sources; state versions and dates).
06-http-semantics-caching-and-real-time-patterns: method safety, idempotency, cacheability per RFC 9110; status-code contracts (301/302/303/307/308 method-preservation rules, 401 vs 403, 409 vs 412, 429 with Retry-After, 502/503/504); Cache-Control (max-age, s-maxage, no-cache vs no-store, must-revalidate, stale-while-revalidate where standardized), ETag with If-None-Match and If-Match, Vary; HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 multiplexing vs HTTP/3; server-sent events vs WebSockets vs long polling; retry safety. Today: why modern APIs rely on idempotency keys for POST, and how CDNs interpret caching headers (verify any vendor-specific claim or omit).
07-cross-chapter-review-and-network-diagnostics: end-to-end latency counting (DNS + TCP + TLS + HTTP round trips for HTTP/1.1 over TLS 1.3 vs HTTP/3, cold vs warm), diagnosing throughput caps from BDP and rwnd, MTU black holes, retry storms and protocol-contract violations in microservice clients. Each question gives a short realistic scenario with numbers.
